one_liner: Merge-path load-balanced CSR SpMV (SC'16) for CPU and GPU; about 1.2x over MKL on average, wins big on skewed rows.
what_it_does: Reference code for Merrill and Garland's SC'16 merge-based CsrMV. It computes y = A*x directly on standard CSR with no preprocessing or format conversion. The CPU kernel is a single ~60-line OpenMP template (OmpMergeCsrmv in cpu_spmv.cpp). The GPU path calls cub::DeviceSpmv::CsrMV from a bundled CUB snapshot. The repo is a benchmark harness against MKL and cuSPARSE, not a packaged library.
how_it_is_fast: It treats the parallel split as a logical merge of the CSR row-end offsets with the nonzero indices 0..nnz-1. That merge path is cut into equal-length diagonals, one per thread, and each thread binary-searches its start coordinate (MergePathSearch). Every thread gets the same rows+nonzeros work no matter how skewed the row lengths are. Rows that span threads are patched in a carry-out fix-up pass. The gain comes from load balance, not from better memory access per nonzero, so it shows most on power-law or very irregular matrices.
when_to_use: fp64/fp32 CSR SpMV on multicore CPUs where row lengths are highly skewed (circuit, web and graph matrices); the README circuit5M run is 53.6 ms with MKL vs 12.6 ms merge on 48 threads
You need a short, permissively licensed (BSD-3) SpMV kernel to vendor into your own code, with no inspector or format-conversion step
Matrices change every call, so per-matrix preprocessing (HYB, CSR5 tiles, plan-based libraries) would not amortize
As a teaching or reference implementation of merge-path decomposition for other segmented reductions
when_not_to_use: Regular, well-balanced matrices (FEM stencils): the paper's minimum is 0.51x vs MKL, and open issue #5 (Dec 2025) reports it 4x slower than plain row-parallel SpMV inside a CG solver on 6 threads
Small matrices on GPU: harmonic mean 0.79x vs cuSPARSE CsrMV for matrices with 300K nnz or fewer on the K40
Modern CUDA: the GPU path relies on cub::DeviceSpmv, which CCCL 2.8 deprecates ('Use the cuSPARSE library instead') and which is gone from CCCL 3.0
If you need a maintained library: no commits since 2017, and the build expects icpc 16 + MKL and CUDA 7.5-era nvcc (open build issues #2 and #3)

integration.dependencies: CPU kernel: OpenMP only (the harness also links MKL and libnuma for comparison); GPU: bundled CUB snapshot, CUDA runtime, cuSPARSE for the comparison
integration.min_toolchain: Tested with icpc 16.0.1 and nvcc 7.5 + gcc 4.4.7; the CPU kernel is plain C++ plus OpenMP
integration.platforms: CPU: x86-64 as tested (Intel AVX Xeon); GPU: NVIDIA compute capability 3.5+
integration.thread_safety: Not documented; the kernel is a pure function of its inputs with stack-local carry arrays
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial: same CSR input and output as mkl csrmv or cusparse csrmv, but you call the template function directly; there is no MKL- or cuSPARSE-compatible API

gotchas: The CPU kernel uses fixed row_carry_out[256] and value_carry_out[256] stack arrays, so more than 256 OpenMP threads overflows them
Merge coordinates and diagonals are int/int2, so rows+nnz must stay below 2^31
The kernel computes y = A*x only (no alpha/beta), and the cross-thread fix-up is a serial loop after the parallel region
The paper names the CPU as Xeon E5-2690 v2 while the README and artifact appendix say E5-2695 v2
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it over CSR5 when you want to keep plain CSR with zero preprocessing and need a tiny vendorable kernel; CSR5 needs a format transform but reported higher averages on its irregular set. Pick it over ISpMV when you need open source or commercial use, or when the matrix changes too often to amortize a plan.
verified_claims_summary: SC'16 paper over 4,201 SuiteSparse matrices, fp64. CPU, built with icpc 16 -O3 -xHost on dual Xeon E5-2690/2695 v2: harmonic-mean 1.21x vs MKL CsrMV (range 0.51-15.8x), 1.26x for the NUMA variant. GPU on a Tesla K40 with CUDA 7.5: 0.84x vs cuSPARSE CsrMV overall (1.13x on matrices above 300K nnz) and 1.29x vs cuSPARSE HybMV.
status_note: Abandoned since February 2017 but BSD-3 licensed. The CPU kernel is small enough to copy; the GPU path is better taken from its CUB lineage (deprecated in CCCL 2.8, removed in 3.0) or replaced by current cuSPARSE.
